sceneHappening: Stephen's speech to the council, and the first martyr
summary: The high priest asks, "Are these things so?" Stephen answers with Israel's story. "The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia," and called him out to a land he would be shown, promising it to his offspring, though he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length. Abraham's descendants would be strangers in a foreign land and be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years. Jacob's sons, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt, "but God was with him," and made him ruler over Egypt, and Jacob and his sons came to Egypt in famine and were buried in Shechem. As the time of the promise drew near, the people grew in Egypt until another king arose who didn't know Joseph. At that time Moses was born, "beautiful to God," brought up in Pharaoh's house, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and powerful in words and deeds. When he was forty he visited his brothers and, seeing one wronged, struck down the Egyptian; he supposed his brothers would understand that God was giving them rescue by his hand, but they didn't. The next day he tried to reconcile two fighting, and one said, "Who made you a ruler and a judge over us?" Moses fled to Midian, and after forty years an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Sinai in the flame of a burning bush: "I am the God of your fathers." "This Moses, whom they refused, saying, 'Who made you a ruler and a judge?' God has sent him to be both a ruler and a deliverer." He led them out, doing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. It was he who said, "God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me," and who received living oracles to give to us. "Our fathers wouldn't be obedient to him, but rejected him, and turned back in their hearts to Egypt," making a calf. God turned and gave them up to serve the army of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets. "Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness," and brought it with Joshua; David asked to find a dwelling for the God of Jacob, but Solomon built him a house. "However the Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says, 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?'" Then, addressing the council: "You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers; you received the law as it was ordained by angels, and did not keep it." When they hear these things they are cut to the heart and gnash their teeth at him. But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looks up steadfastly into heaven and sees the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and says, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!" They cry out with a loud voice, stop their ears, rush at him with one accord, cast him out of the city, and stone him. The witnesses lay down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. They stone Stephen as he calls out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!" and kneeling down he cries with a loud voice, "Lord, don't hold this sin against them!" Having said this, he falls asleep, and Saul is consenting to his death.
whySettingMatters: Stephen's speech is the longest in Acts, and it does not directly answer the charges; it retells Israel's history to argue that God has never been confined to one place, whether Mesopotamia, Egypt, Midian, Sinai, or the temple, and that Israel has repeatedly resisted those God sent, from Joseph to Moses to the prophets. A few details in his account differ from the Old Testament, such as where Abraham was buried and how many people went into Egypt, and how to explain the differences is debated, though many are variations that reflect the Greek Old Testament or other Jewish traditions. His critique of the temple ("not made with hands") quotes Isaiah 66:1-2 and is the sharpest charge in the speech; the same phrase is used by Paul in 17:24. "Stiff-necked" and "uncircumcised in heart" are phrases the prophets used against Israel (Exodus 32:9, Jeremiah 9:26). Stephen's vision of Jesus "standing" at God's right hand, not sitting as in Psalm 110, may show him as witness or advocate. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16); Roman governors usually kept the right of capital punishment, and whether this was a trial or a lynching is debated. Stephen's words, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" and "don't hold this sin against them," echo Jesus' last words in Luke 23:34 and 23:46. The young man Saul is introduced here, minding the coats.

questions: Stephen answers a question about the temple with Israel's history. Why do you think he does that?
"Heaven is my throne." How does that challenge ideas of where God is found?
Stephen sees Jesus standing. What difference does it make that Jesus is standing, not sitting?
Stephen's last words echo Jesus'. What is Luke showing us about how followers of Jesus die?
